pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** Extinction & Rapid Change — how environmental change can outpace a species' ability to adapt through natural selection, leading to extinction, using historical and contemporary examples

- **Standards — UK (DfE Key Stage 3, Biology — Genetics and evolution):** changes in the environment may leave individuals within a species, and some entire species, less well adapted to compete successfully and reproduce, which in turn may lead to extinction.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS4-1):** analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS4-1]; (MS-LS2-4) argue from evidence that changes to an ecosystem's components affect populations.

- **Operational details:** This is the most-central node in the domain — it ties the whole spine together: natural selection (mechanism), variation/mutation (raw material), environmental change (driver), and interdependence (consequence) all converge here. The load-bearing idea is a RACE OF RATES: adaptation by natural selection needs many generations and pre-existing heritable variation; when the environment changes FASTER than a population can track it — or when no suitable variation exists to select — the population declines and can go extinct. Make the rate comparison explicit and quantitative in feel: a slow-breeding, specialised species with little genetic variation adapts slowly and is most vulnerable; a fast-breeding, variable generalist can sometimes keep pace. Teach the distinction between BACKGROUND extinction (the steady, low, ongoing rate) and MASS extinction (rare, catastrophic pulses like the K–Pg asteroid). Use a historical case (dodo — flightless, island-endemic, hunted and preyed on by introduced animals it had no defences against; woolly mammoth — warming plus hunting) and a contemporary case (amphibians, coral, or a named endangered species) to show the same rate-mismatch logic across time. Close on the present: human activity (habitat loss, hunting, pollution, climate change) is driving change fast enough that current extinction rates far exceed background — the 'sixth mass extinction' framing — linking evolution directly to the pupil's world and to conservation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/systems-relational). Pupils can reason about competing rates, thresholds, and the interaction of multiple drivers, and marshal evidence into an argument. Success = explaining extinction as change outpacing adaptation, giving a historical and a contemporary example, distinguishing background from mass extinction, and explaining how human activity accelerates current species loss.
bestPractices: Frame extinction as a RACE OF RATES — speed of environmental change vs speed of adaptation — rather than a species simply 'failing' or being 'weak'.
Make vulnerability factors explicit (generation time, genetic variation, degree of specialism) so pupils can predict which species survive rapid change and which don't.
Distinguish background extinction (steady, ongoing) from mass extinction (rare catastrophic pulses) using a geological timeline.
Pair a historical case (dodo, mammoth) with a contemporary one (amphibians, coral) to show the same rate-mismatch logic across time.
Explicitly integrate the spine: extinction is where variation, mutation, natural selection, environmental change and interdependence all meet — use it to consolidate the domain.
Land the topic in the present with the human-driven sixth-extinction framing, connecting evolution to conservation and the pupil's own world.
keyRepresentations: A rate-race display: adaptation (trait distribution shifting) vs environmental change, with population size falling when change wins
A 'hall of extinction' gallery of extinct/endangered species with their vulnerability factors
A geological timeline marking the five mass extinctions and the current pulse
A vulnerability matrix (fast vs slow breeder, high vs low variation, specialist vs generalist)
Background-rate trickle vs mass-extinction spike comparison
commonMisconceptions: Thinking extinct species were simply 'weak', 'lazy' or 'failed to try', rather than unable to adapt fast enough to change.
Believing a species can adapt on demand within a generation or two when the environment changes suddenly.
Assuming extinction is always caused by a single dramatic event (asteroid), missing gradual and multi-driver causes.
Confusing background extinction with mass extinction, or thinking extinction is entirely abnormal rather than a constant low-level process.
Thinking humans are separate from these processes, rather than the primary driver of the current accelerated extinction rate.
Believing that because life recovered after past mass extinctions, current biodiversity loss is nothing to worry about — ignoring the million-year recovery timescales.

learn.summary: For ages 12–14: teach extinction as a RACE OF RATES — the speed of environmental change versus the speed at which a population can adapt by natural selection — rather than a species being 'weak' or 'failing to try'. Learners manipulate both rates for the same population, see selection track slow change but lose the race under fast change, explore vulnerability factors (generation time, genetic variation, specialism), distinguish background from mass extinction, and connect the reasoning to human-driven present-day losses. A role-play argument and a case gallery deepen and extend the core model. The simulation is one representation among several, not a uniquely necessary or proven-superior medium.

activities.title: The survival race: dial the rate of change against the rate of adaptation
feedback: When the population survives slow change: 'Selection kept pace — the trait distribution shifted each generation fast enough to track the environment.'
When it crashes under fast change: 'Selection lost the race. Adaptation needs pre-existing variation and many generations; the environment changed faster than the population could follow.'

If a learner treats a few remaining individuals as a guarantee of recovery: 'A population can be doomed before the last individual dies — too few individuals means too little variation and breeding capacity (minimum viable population).'

When comparing specialist vs generalist: 'Same change rate, different outcome — short generations and more variation let the generalist track change faster, and its broader needs meant it had less adapting to do than the specialist.'
activities.rationale: The load-bearing idea is a comparison of two rates over time; letting learners vary each rate independently for the same population is intended to make the mechanism visible and to surface the 'species just evolves on demand' and 'extinct = weak' misconceptions. A simulation is proposed as one medium that may make this rate comparison visible, not the only possible one, and no proven effectiveness is claimed for this specific activity.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn that changes in the environment may leave individuals and entire species less well adapted to compete and reproduce, which may lead to extinction.
learnerActions: Start a scenario where a population with heritable variation faces a changing environment (e.g. gradual warming, or a newly arrived predator) and set the environmental change to a slow rate.
Watch two linked displays at once: the trait distribution shifting generation by generation via selection, and the total population size over time.
Observe that under slow change, selection tracks the environment, the trait distribution slides to match, and the population holds steady — the species survives.

Push the rate-of-change slider higher and watch selection fall behind: the trait distribution cannot shift fast enough, numbers plunge, and the population reaches EXTINCT — the very same species that survived slow change.

Handicap the species using vulnerability levers — long generation time, little genetic variation, high specialism — and compare, in the model, how a slow-breeding, low-variation specialist dies out where a fast-breeding, variable generalist scrapes through at the same rate of change.
Switch into a 'background vs mass' comparison: a steady low trickle of extinctions versus a sudden catastrophic pulse, and note the different pattern each produces.
Press a 'switch to today's rate' option to see how current extinction rates, driven largely by human-caused change, compare with the background extinction rate.
activities.intendedInsight: Extinction can happen when environmental change outpaces the generations-long, variation-dependent process of adaptation — a mismatch of rates, not a species simply being weak or failing. Which species survive rapid change depends partly on generation time, available heritable variation, and degree of specialism (as well as factors such as population size and ability to disperse).

activities.title: Argue the case: interview a conservation biologist or palaeontologist
feedback: Reward answers that tie survival to change being slower than the generational adaptation rate given available variation.
Challenge answers that say a species 'failed' or 'was weak' — redirect to the rate comparison and specific vulnerability factors.
Prompt for a human-driver when the learner explains current losses only in terms of natural change.
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive dialogue lets a learner construct and defend reasoning in their own words rather than only recognise it, which serves the argue-from-evidence objective; recognition tasks alone do not elicit this production. Best used as a debrief after the model-building activity; it is one proposed medium, not a required one, and no proven effectiveness is claimed.

Extinction results when environmental change outpaces adaptation; current extinction rates far exceed the background rate, and human activity (habitat loss, overexploitation, pollution, climate change) is the primary driver of the present biodiversity crisis (often termed the sixth mass extinction).
learnerActions: Take part in a role-play interview with a palaeontologist (about the dodo or woolly mammoth) or a conservation biologist (about a species on the brink today).
Respond to the challenge 'Why couldn't it just adapt?' by explaining the rate mismatch and the species' specific vulnerability factors.

Respond to 'Why are today's extinction rates different from normal?' by distinguishing background from mass extinction and naming human drivers (habitat loss, overexploitation, pollution, climate change).
Marshal observations from the survival-race activity into a short, evidence-based argument about whether a named species can keep pace with current change.
activities.intendedInsight: The argue-from-evidence objective asks learners to turn the rate-race model into a defended explanation of why a given species could not keep pace and why current rates exceed the background rate.

activities.title: Hall of extinction: case gallery and geological timeline
feedback: Confirm correct vulnerability reasoning, e.g. 'The dodo was flightless, island-endemic and had no defences against introduced predators, with little chance to adapt in time.'
If a learner treats all extinction as caused by a single asteroid-style event, highlight gradual and multi-driver cases on the timeline.
If background and mass extinction are confused, contrast the steady trickle with the catastrophic spike on the timeline.
activities.rationale: A richly annotated gallery and timeline present the cases and vocabulary and support categorisation and justification. As a fixed resource it presents examples well but does not itself let learners run the rate comparison, so it works best as pre-teaching or reference alongside the modelling activity. The sort can check and support classification but does not itself elicit the rate-race reasoning or a spoken explanation.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn that changes in the environment may leave individuals and entire species less well adapted to compete and reproduce, which may lead to extinction.
learnerActions: Explore a gallery of extinct and endangered species — dodo, woolly mammoth, thylacine, plus contemporary cases such as amphibians or coral — revealing for each one its vulnerability factors and the specific change that outpaced it.
Place each case on a geological timeline that marks the five past mass extinctions and the current pulse.
For each species, state in your own words what outpaced its ability to adapt and why.
Sort species into higher or lower vulnerability and justify each choice using generation time, genetic variation, and specialism.
activities.intendedInsight: The same rate-mismatch logic explains extinctions across deep time and the present; vulnerability factors help predict which species survive rapid change. Background extinction is a steady ongoing process, distinct from rare catastrophic mass-extinction pulses.

activities.title: Check and apply: diagnostic on 'animals will just evolve in time'
feedback: Full response: explains extinction as change outpacing the generational rate of adaptation given available variation, distinguishes background from mass extinction and endangered from extinct, links current losses to human drivers, and transfers the reasoning to the slow-versus-fast case.

Partial response: recognises that fast change is dangerous but cannot tie it to the mechanism, or cannot distinguish background from mass extinction, or endangered from extinct — reteach by comparing a fast and slow version of the same change.
Gap response endorsing 'animals always evolve quickly enough': tie adaptation to its requirements (pre-existing heritable variation and many generations); evolution is not an on-demand rescue.

If a learner says individuals will remodel their own bodies because they need to: any change within a lifetime is limited and not inherited; adaptation comes from selection acting across generations on heritable variation (mostly already present, with new mutations arising at random), and only if there is time — need does not trigger the right change.

If a learner treats 30 surviving individuals as 'saved': introduce minimum viable population — too few individuals means too little variation, inbreeding and vulnerability to chance events, so a species can be doomed before the last one dies; it is far from safe, even though intensive captive breeding has occasionally rescued species from very low numbers (e.g. California condor).
activities.rationale: The diagnostic and its distractor map onto the documented on-demand-evolution misconception: learners who hold it endorse the claim while those who grasp the rate argument reject it, giving a discriminating check. The match and distinguish steps check recognition and categorisation; the open explanation requires learners to construct reasoning. Probing with a slow-versus-fast variant tests transfer of the mechanism.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn that changes in the environment may leave individuals and entire species less well adapted to compete and reproduce, which may lead to extinction.
learnerActions: Judge the claim: 'As the climate warms very fast, don't worry — animals will just evolve quickly to cope, so they won't go extinct.' Decide whether the reasoning is sound and explain when a species CAN adapt in time and when it can't.
Answer the follow-up: the same warming happens slowly over 50,000 years instead of 100 years — does your answer change, and why?
Answer: there are 30 individuals of a species left, all in one zoo — is that species safe? Why or why not?
Explain how the current rate of extinction differs from the background rate and what is driving the difference.
Match each historical case to what outpaced it, and distinguish an example of background extinction from a mass extinction.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who grasps the rate argument rejects 'just evolve in time', ties survival to change being slower than the generational adaptation rate given available variation, separates endangered from extinct (minimum viable population), and separates background from mass extinction.

constraints: Keep the rate comparison explicit: when a population cannot move away or simply tolerate the change, its survival depends on the environment changing slowly enough for its generation-and-variation-limited adaptation to keep up. Real populations may sometimes persist by dispersing to suitable habitat, and some extinctions have direct causes such as overhunting. Do not let learners conclude adaptation happens on demand within a generation or two.

Correct the teleological error directly: individuals cannot evolve, and any adjustment within a lifetime (such as acclimatisation) is limited and not inherited; need does not summon the right mutation. Adaptation by natural selection acts across generations on heritable variation, which is mostly already present plus new random mutations that arise whatever the need, and it only works if there is time.
Distinguish endangered from extinct using minimum viable population: a species can be doomed before the last individual dies, so a few surviving individuals does not mean recovery.

Build in the distinction between background extinction (steady, low, ongoing) and mass extinction (rare catastrophic pulses); do not imply extinction is wholly abnormal or always caused by a single dramatic event.
Include at least one historical and one contemporary case so the same rate-mismatch logic is seen across time.

The case gallery and timeline present examples and vocabulary but cannot themselves run the rate comparison; pair them with the active modelling and the argument task rather than relying on them alone.

The simulation and slider controls are one concrete way to make the rate race visible, not the only valid medium; the objective is for learners to reason about and argue the competing rates, however represented. No claim of proven effectiveness is made for these specific activities.
Avoid implying that because life recovered after past mass extinctions current biodiversity loss is unimportant — recovery took millions of years.

Multiple-choice and matching checks assess recognition and categorisation; independent explanation and argument (the argue-from-evidence standard) require learners to construct and defend reasoning in their own words.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical testing of these specific activities is claimed.

Two of the three cited sources carry verified:false in the source row (NGSS MS-LS4-1 and the IPBES claim); their evidence status was not independently confirmed here. Treat the 'sixth mass extinction' framing and current-rate comparisons as attributed claims, not independently re-verified facts.

The source's '3D adds nothing / coded 2D sim can pit rates against each other directly' framing was softened: a simulation is presented as one medium that may make the temporal rate comparison visible, not the uniquely necessary one.

The original scenario numbers and examples (e.g. 50,000 years vs 100 years, 30 individuals in a zoo) were retained as written; they are illustrative teaching scenarios, not precise empirical values, and should be reviewed for the intended teaching register.

No arithmetic or force/motion claims were present to re-audit; the main conceptual risk checked was ensuring adaptation is not portrayed as on-demand or teleological, which the activities and constraints address explicitly.
activity[0].feedback was adjusted so the minimum-viable-population feedback is triggered by the survivor/recovery assumption it actually corrects, rather than by a 'recover quickly' expectation.

The NGSS MS-LS4-1 claim on activity[1] is retained as support for the evidence-analysis/argue-from-evidence objective engaged by the fossil-record cases, not as evidence that the dialogue medium is necessary or tested; a stricter reviewer could trim it to the KS3/IPBES claims.

probeDeeper: The same warming happens slowly over 50,000 years instead of 100 years — does your answer change? Why?
There are 30 individuals of a species left, all in one zoo — is that species safe? Why or why not?
How is the current rate of extinction different from the 'background' rate, and what's driving the difference?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Adaptation by natural selection needs pre-existing heritable variation and many generations; a species can only keep up if the environment changes slower than that. When change is very fast — or the population is small with little variation, or slow to breed — it can't produce the adaptations in time and goes extinct. Evolution isn't an on-demand rescue; it can't be summoned just because it's needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Evolution-on-demand rescue — 'species always evolve fast enough to survive; they'll adapt to anything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie adaptation to its requirements: it needs existing heritable variation and many generations; if change outpaces that, there's no rescue. Compare a fast versus slow version of the same change.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — animals always evolve quickly enough to cope, so they won't go extinct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees animals will simply evolve in time, treating adaptation as guaranteed and instant

errorPatterns.pattern: Teleological adaptation — 'they'll change their bodies because they need to'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Remove will and purpose: individuals can't remodel themselves to fit; only selection on existing variation across generations can shift a population, and only if there's time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says individuals will change themselves to cope, or that the need triggers the right change

errorPatterns.pattern: Endangered = extinct / a few survivors means saved
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce minimum viable population: too few individuals means too little genetic variation and breeding capacity, so a species can be doomed even before the last one dies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats any surviving individuals as recovery, ignoring minimum viable population; uses 'endangered' and 'extinct' interchangeably

responseLevels.gap: Says species will always evolve in time; treats evolution as guaranteed or on-demand, or endangered as the same as safe.
responseLevels.full: Explains extinction as change outpacing the generational rate of adaptation given available variation, distinguishes background from mass extinction and endangered from extinct (minimum viable population), links current losses to human drivers, and applies the rate reasoning to a new slow-versus-fast case.
responseLevels.partial: Says fast change is dangerous and can cause extinction, but can't tie it to the mechanism (adaptation needs existing variation and many generations relative to the rate of change), or can't distinguish background from mass extinction, or endangered from extinct.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: As the climate warms very fast, someone says: 'Don't worry — animals will just evolve quickly to cope with the heat, so they won't go extinct.' Is that reasoning sound? Explain when a species CAN adapt in time and when it can't.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps the rate argument rejects the 'just evolve in time' claim and ties survival to change being slower than the generational adaptation rate. A child holding the 'evolution always rescues' idea endorses it — opposite answers, and the distractor is the documented on-demand-evolution misconception.
